meaning: This first branch of the chapter asks what a Bitcoin wallet really contains and where its keys come from
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node

meaning: Wallet contents is the group of ideas that answer a simple question: what is inside a Bitcoin wallet, and what is not? It collects three concepts
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; panel WalletContents

meaning: The wallet database is the stored collection of keys (and the notes about them) that a wallet application reads and writes; it holds the means to prove control of bitcoins, not the bitcoins themselves.
analogy: A key ring in a drawer, with a notebook beside it
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: A wallet database that holds public keys but not the private keys can recognise payments and create receiving addresses but cannot sign a spending transaction.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node

meaning: In external signing the wallet application builds a transaction and another party, a hardware signing device or the other signers of a multisignature scheme, holds the private keys and returns the signature.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node

meaning: Key generation methods are the ways a wallet application produces the key pairs that it will later distribute and use
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; panel KeyGenerationMethods

meaning: In independent key generation every key is created separately from random data, so every key has to be saved on its own and the backup is out of date after each new key.
analogy: Cutting a new, unrelated key for every door
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: A seed is the random value from which a deterministic wallet derives all its keys; the same seed, with the same algorithm, always gives the same keys.
analogy: The master recipe card kept in a safe
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: Deterministic key generation computes keys from a seed by a fixed rule, such as hashing the seed with a counter, so the same seed always yields the same keys.
analogy: A recipe: the same ingredients give the same dish
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: A key tweak is a value added to a public key, and in the same way to its private key, so that the child public key can be computed by someone who does not know the private key.
analogy: A copy of a key filed down by a fixed amount
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: Hierarchical deterministic (HD) key generation, the standard BIP32, derives a tree of keys from one seed; any key can be the parent of further keys, and public keys can be derived without private keys.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: A recovery code is the short, written form of a wallet's seed: a sequence of words, or in one case a string of letters and digits, from which every key of a deterministic wallet can be computed again
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node

meaning: This group describes the recovery code schemes themselves
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; panel CodeSchemes

meaning: A BIP39 recovery code is a sequence of 12 to 24 words that encodes a random number together with a short checksum, from which a 512-bit seed is derived; the standard was published in 2013 and is the most widely used scheme.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: The Electrum version 2 scheme derives both the master private key and a version number from a hash of the normalised phrase, so it needs no fixed word list and can tell an old code from a new one.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: The Aezeed scheme of the lnd wallet enciphers a plaintext of version, timestamp and entropy into a 24-word code, so the passphrase is authenticated and the code can be upgraded or re-enciphered.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: The Muun recovery code is not words and is not the seed: it is a key that decrypts the private keys held in a document the wallet gives the user, which suits a wallet whose spending needs several signatures.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node

meaning: SLIP39 splits one seed into several word codes with a threshold, so that any sufficient subset recovers the seed and any smaller subset reveals nothing about it.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: codex32 writes a BIP32 master seed in the bech32 alphabet with an error-correcting checksum that can be verified by hand, and can split the seed into up to 31 shares with a threshold between 2 and 9.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: This group gathers the decisions that are not settled by choosing a scheme
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; panel CodeTradeoffs

meaning: A passphrase is an extra secret that is mixed into the derivation of the seed, so that one recovery code yields a different wallet for every passphrase and the code alone is not enough to spend.
analogy: A second lock on the safe
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: Plausible deniability is the property that a revealed recovery code or passphrase always looks valid, so a holder cannot be shown to have withheld anything - which protects and endangers them at the same time.
analogy: A decoy purse with a little cash
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: A brainwallet is a wallet whose keys come from a phrase the user chose, which is insecure because people are poor sources of randomness; a recovery code is generated by the wallet instead.
analogy: A password you invented, not a random one
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: Memorising a code is possible because the code is words, and is dangerous because memory fails, cannot be inherited and can be coerced; the chapter recommends writing the code down as well.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: Because a recovery code is all that is needed to spend, people who are believed to hold one have been attacked in person; the chapter cites a public list of such cases and the list has grown since.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node

meaning: A wallet birthday is the creation date recorded inside a recovery code, so that a restoration can scan the blockchain from that date instead of from the beginning.
analogy: The date the safe was bought
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: This branch opens the second half of the chapter, in which the book stops surveying the options and works through one stack of technologies in detail
slide visual: code; drawn shapes; native chart; table
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node

meaning: This group follows the first six steps of BIP39
analogy: Shuffle the deck, then write the card order down
slide visual: code; drawn shapes; native chart; table
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; panel CodeGeneration

meaning: Entropy is the unpredictability of a value, measured in bits; a BIP39 code encodes 128 to 256 bits of it, drawn by the wallet from a source of randomness and not chosen by a person.
analogy: A deck shuffled so well nobody can guess it
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; chapter visual Entropy; lab example

meaning: The BIP39 checksum is the first entropy-length over 32 bits of the SHA-256 hash of the entropy, appended to it, so that a mistyped code can be detected but not corrected.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: The BIP39 word list holds exactly 2,048 words, so that each word stands for 11 bits; the list is sorted, has unique four-letter prefixes and avoids similar pairs.
analogy: A numbered dictionary everyone shares
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: The entropy and checksum are read as consecutive groups of 11 bits, each group a number from 0 to 2,047 that selects one word of the list.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: Entropy length, checksum length and word count are tied together: the checksum is a thirty-second of the entropy and the total divided by 11 is the number of words, so codes have 12, 15, 18, 21 or 24 words.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; chapter visual CodeLength; lab example

meaning: Normalisation rewrites text in a single canonical form before it is hashed, so that two spellings a person cannot distinguish produce the same bytes and therefore the same seed.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

concept: From the code to the seed
meaning: This group covers the last three of BIP39's nine steps, the ones that turn words back into the number a wallet actually uses
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; panel SeedDerivation

meaning: A key-stretching function derives a key from a secret deliberately slowly, by repeating a hash many times, so that each guess an attacker makes costs more.
analogy: Kneading dough again and again
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: PBKDF2 is the standard password-based key derivation function that BIP39 uses: it applies HMAC-SHA512 2,048 times to the words and the salt and returns 64 bytes.
analogy: A kneading machine set to 2,048 turns
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: A salt is the second, non-secret input of a key derivation function; BIP39's salt is the string mnemonic followed by the optional passphrase, which is how the passphrase changes the seed.
analogy: A pinch of spice that makes each dish unique
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: The root seed is the value from which every key of a hierarchical deterministic wallet is derived; BIP39 produces one of 512 bits, and BIP32 accepts 128 to 512.
analogy: The first seed from which the garden grows
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: In BIP39 the optional passphrase is appended to the constant salt, so any passphrase yields a different valid seed from the same words and none of them is wrong.
analogy: A second combination on the same padlock
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: Security strength is the work an attacker needs, measured in bits; extended keys hold 512 bits, private keys 256, and the elliptic curve offers about 128, so more than 128 bits of entropy buys little.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: A hierarchical deterministic wallet, which the chapter and the standards abbreviate to HD wallet, is a wallet whose keys form a tree, every node of which is computed from the seed
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node

meaning: This group covers the one step that turns a seed into the root of a key tree
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; panel MasterKeys

meaning: HMAC-SHA512 is a keyed hash: it combines a key and a message into 64 bytes that cannot be produced without the key, and BIP32 uses it both to make the master keys and to derive every child.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: The master private key is the left 32 bytes of HMAC-SHA512 over the seed, read as a 256-bit number; it is the root of the tree and is written m.
analogy: The ancestor's key at the top of the tree
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: The master chain code is the right 32 bytes of HMAC-SHA512 over the seed: 256 bits of extra entropy that make every derivation depend on more than the key.
analogy: The ancestor's secret handshake
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: This group covers the functions that make a child key from a parent
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; panel ChildDerivation

meaning: A child is derived by hashing the parent key, the parent chain code and an index with HMAC-SHA512 and splitting the 512-bit result: the left half makes the child key, the right half is the child chain code.
analogy: A child born from a parent and a birth number
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: A chain code is the 32 bytes of extra entropy carried beside a key so that derivation depends on more than the key; a key's children cannot be found without it.
analogy: A family secret passed down each generation
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: The index is the 32-bit number that selects which child is derived; indices below 2 to the 31 are normal children and those at or above it are hardened, displayed with an apostrophe or an h.
analogy: Birth order: first child, second child
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: A private child is the sum, modulo the order of the curve, of the parent private key and the left half of the derivation hash; the right half is the child's chain code.
analogy: A parent handing a child their own key
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: Hardened derivation feeds the parent private key, not the parent public key, into the hash, so the resulting chain code cannot be used with a leaked child key to recover the parent.
analogy: A firewall between parent and child
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: A public child can be derived from a parent public key and chain code alone, because adding a value to a public key gives the public key of the sum, so a server can make addresses without the power to spend.
analogy: Numbering doors without holding any key
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: A child key on its own behaves exactly like a randomly generated key: it can make a public key, an address and signatures, but it cannot find its parent, its siblings or its own children.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: This group is about the object a wallet actually passes around
analogy: A key with its family notes stapled on
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; panel ExtendedKeys

meaning: An extended key is a key together with its chain code, stored as the two concatenated; it is the root of a branch and is what a derivation function needs.
analogy: A key with its family notes stapled on
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: An extended private key is a private key with its chain code; it can derive every descendant key, private and public, and is written with the prefix xprv.
analogy: The archive where every door opens
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: An extended public key is a public key with its chain code: it derives all the normal public keys of its branch and none of the private ones, and is written with the prefix xpub.
analogy: A guest list that greets visitors but opens no doors
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: An extended key is written in base58check with four version bytes, which is what produces the recognisable xprv and xpub prefixes and a fixed length of 111 characters.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: A key fingerprint is the first four bytes of the hash identifier of an extended key, used as a short, non-unique label for the parent a derivation started from.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: This group is about saying which key of the tree is meant
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; panel TreeNavigation

meaning: A key path names a key by the sequence of indices from the root, written with slashes, beginning m for private or M for public keys, with a prime or h for hardened steps.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: BIP43 reserves the first hardened level of a BIP32 tree for a purpose number that says which scheme the rest of the tree follows, and recommends using the scheme's own BIP number.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: BIP44 defines the five levels purpose, coin type, account, change and address index under purpose 44 hardened, with the first three hardened and the last two normal.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: The account level is the third level of a BIP44 path, hardened, which splits a wallet into independent subaccounts that never mix coins.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: The fourth level of a BIP44 path is 0 for the external chain, whose addresses are given out, and 1 for the internal chain, which receives change; both use normal derivation.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: The fifth level of a BIP44 path is the address index, counted from zero with normal derivation, and it is the level a wallet advances each time it needs a new address.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: This branch is about the part of a backup that a recovery code does not contain
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node

meaning: This group covers the two ways of knowing which paths a wallet used
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; panel PathConventions

meaning: An implicit path is a standardised derivation path that a wallet uses without being told, so that nothing has to be backed up beside the recovery code - at the price of inflexibility.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: An explicit path is derivation information backed up alongside the recovery code, which says exactly which keys go with which scripts and can carry extra data such as other people's public keys.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: BIP44's account path for pay-to-public-key-hash scripts is the first of the standard implicit paths and the one the chapter's table gives for legacy addresses.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: BIP49 gives segregated witness keys wrapped in a script hash their own account path, so that an incompatible wallet finds nothing rather than finding part of the funds.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: BIP84 gives native segregated witness keys their own account path, and its test vector's first address is the bech32 address the course can recompute from the key hash.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: BIP86 gives single-key taproot outputs their own account path and says how the output key is computed from the derived key by a tagged hash.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: A multisignature arrangement requires several of a set of keys to sign; its participants cannot restore the arrangement from their own seeds alone, because they also need the others' public keys.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: This group covers the notation in which explicit paths are written
analogy: A recipe card naming the dish and its ingredients
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; panel Descriptors

meaning: An output script is the program in a transaction output that says what must be presented to spend it; a descriptor is a description of a family of such scripts.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: A descriptor is a short expression naming a script type as a function and its keys as arguments, so that it says exactly which scripts and addresses a wallet should produce.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: A descriptor carries an eight-character error-detecting checksum after a hash sign, which catches any one or two symbol errors in a descriptor of ordinary length.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: The key origin of a descriptor records, in brackets, the fingerprint of the master key and the path from it to the key that follows, so that a signing device can find the right key.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: A multipath descriptor writes a tuple of derivation steps in angle brackets, so that one descriptor stands for the receive and the change descriptor of a wallet.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: Miniscript is a structured language for a subset of Bitcoin scripts, so that spending conditions can be analysed, composed and signed for; descriptors can contain it.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

concept: Backing up data that is not keys
meaning: This branch is about everything in a wallet that a seed cannot reproduce
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node

meaning: This group covers the information a user adds to a wallet by hand
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; panel WalletNotes

meaning: An address label is a note a user attaches to an address they hand out, so that payments arriving there can be recognised; it exists only in that user's wallet.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: A transaction label is a note a user attaches to a payment they made or received, which a seed-based restoration cannot reproduce.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: BIP329 proposes a line-based JSON format for exporting wallet labels, so that labels can be moved between applications instead of locking a user into one.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: This group covers the data that protocols built on top of Bitcoin add to a wallet, and the one general solution the chapter offers for backing everything up
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; panel OtherProtocolData

meaning: The Lightning Network is a protocol of payment channels built on Bitcoin, in which funds live in outputs that two parties control jointly, so a wallet must keep state that no seed can reproduce.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node

meaning: A static channel backup records what is needed to recover a channel's settled funds and is taken once, when the channel is created; it allows recovery of those funds but cannot guarantee the result.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node

meaning: Encryption turns data into a form that only a holder of the key can read back; a wallet can therefore store a backup where anyone can see it, as long as the key stays secret.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: An encrypted wallet backup is a complete copy of the wallet database, encrypted under a key derived from the seed, which a user can restore from a recovery code alone.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: This branch is the chapter's extended worked example and its practical advice
slide visual: code; drawn shapes; native chart; picture; table
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node

concept: An extended key on a web store
meaning: This group follows the chapter's web store example and the one new idea it needs
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; panel WebStore

meaning: Deploying an extended public key means putting the watching half of a wallet on an exposed computer, which can then derive a fresh address for every order and spend nothing.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: The gap limit is the number of unused addresses in a row that a wallet will tolerate before it stops looking for payments; a payment beyond it is not found.
analogy: Checking mailboxes until a set number in a row are empty
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: A payment processor is the program that watches for payments and matches them to orders; a self-hosted one lets a merchant accept bitcoins with the extended public key as its only key material.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node

meaning: This group covers the other half of every arrangement in the chapter: where the private keys are when they are not in use
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; panel OfflineKeys

meaning: Cold storage means keeping keys offline, created and stored in a secure environment that is not connected to a network, so that an attack on a connected computer cannot reach them.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node

meaning: A hardware signing device stores private keys and produces signatures on request without revealing the keys, so a less secure computer can build transactions it cannot sign.
analogy: A notary who stamps letters and never hands over the stamp
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node

meaning: A written backup is the recovery code on paper, which the chapter recommends even for schemes designed to be memorised, because memory fails and cannot be inherited.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: This last branch collects the ideas that the rest of the chapter uses as though they were already known
slide visual: code; drawn shapes; native chart; table
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node

meaning: A cryptographic primitive is a basic operation out of which protocols are built: this group covers the four that chapter 5 uses
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; panel CryptographicPrimitives

meaning: A hash function maps data of any size to a fixed-size value, always the same for the same input and unpredictable for a changed one, and cannot be run backwards.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: SHA-256 and SHA-512 are the two secure hash algorithms this chapter's standards name, producing 32 and 64 bytes; the choice of one or the other fixes the sizes in every scheme.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: A digital signature is a value computed from a message and a private key that anyone can check against the matching public key, which is how spending a Bitcoin output is authorised.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: Secret sharing splits a secret into parts so that any sufficient number of them recovers it and any smaller number reveals nothing; it is the mathematics behind SLIP39 and codex32.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: This last group turns the chapter's technical content into two statements about practice
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; panel RecoveryPractice

meaning: Data loss is the loss of the keys or of the information needed to use them, which the chapter names as perhaps the leading cause of lost bitcoins, and which no one can reverse.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: Testing a backup means carrying out a recovery before it is needed, which is the only way to learn that a code, a path and the non-key data are all sufficient.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example
